newsitem.title: JAPAN: U.N. battles to budge Japan on N.Korea food aid.
newsitem.headline: U.N. battles to budge Japan on N.Korea food aid.

text.p: U.N. Undersecretary General Yasushi Akashi, a Japanese national, appeared to be facing an uphill battle on Wednesday in convincing his home country to give emergency aid to famine-hit North Korea.

Akashi, visiting Tokyo this week after a tour of North Korea, has called on government and ruling party officials to join international relief efforts to avert famine in Japan's impoverished Stalinist neighbour and former colony.

His call has fallen on deaf ears in Japan, which demands that Pyongyang first address alleged kidnappings of Japanese nationals by North Korean agents and allow Japanese nationals trapped in North Korea to come home.
Although declining to directly criticise Tokyo, he hinted he was disappointed at Tokyo's rigid stance.
"It is a bit strange to see Japan, a leading Asian nation, totally absent from relief efforts in North Korea," Akashi told a news conference.
Although aid has started reaching hungry North Koreans "assistance will continue to be needed at least until the October harvest", he said.

At least 10 Japanese were kidnapped by North Korean agents in the 1970s and 1980s, Japan has said, and thousands of Japanese women who married North Koreans and moved there in the 1960s have not been heard from in decades, their families say.

On Wednesday, the Yomiuri Shimbun, Japan's largest daily, published a poll showing only 22.6 percent of those asked were in favour of sending emergency food aid without preconditions, while 59.4 percent say aid must await the resolution of outstanding issues.
Akashi, head of the U.N. Department of Humanitarian Affairs, acknowledged Japanese concerns, but said food aid should not be tied to politics.

Echoing concerns voiced in South Korea and in Western countries which have provided the bulk of aid to North Korea, most opponents of aid in Japan doubted that food aid would reach ordinary North Koreans.

North Korea had agreed to Akashi's request that it conduct a nutritional survey with U.N and other relief agencies and that it give the U.N. access to the entire country and increase monitoring of aid distribution, he said.
On Tuesday, the U.N. World Food Programme (WFP) said it had almost reached the food aid target of $95.5 million it set for famine-threatened North Korea.
The WFP launched an appeal in May this year to purchase and deliver 203,000 tonnes of emergency food aid to North Korea after it slid into a famine following unprecedented flooding in 1995 and 1996.
